quests.instruction: In “Ines said that that was fine”, how do the two “that” words differ?
quests.word: Ines said that that was fine
quests.textToSpeak: Ines said that that was fine
options: Both are strong, /ðæt/, because they are the same word
The conjunction “that” is weak, /ðət/; the demonstrative is strong, /ðæt/
Both are weak, /ðət/, because neither carries meaning
The first is strong and the second is weak, because the first begins the clause
quests.correctAnswer: The conjunction “that” is weak, /ðət/; the demonstrative is strong, /ðæt/
quests.hint: Decide which “that” introduces a clause and which one points at something.
quests.explanation: The first “that” links “said” to the clause that follows, so it is a function word with the weak form /ðət/. The second “that” is a demonstrative pronoun that refers to something, so it keeps more stress and the vowel /æ/. The same spelling therefore has two spoken forms, decided by its job.
quests.phoneticRule: Words with several grammatical roles may have different strong and weak forms: conjunction “that” is weak, and demonstrative “that” is strong.
quests.spokenForm: Ines sed thət THAT was fine

quests.instruction: In “Jonas, I have a car and I have seen it”, how do the two “have” words differ?
quests.word: Jonas, I have a car and I have seen it
quests.textToSpeak: Jonas, I have a car and I have seen it
options: The main verb “have” keeps /hæv/; the auxiliary “have” is weak, /əv/
Both are weak, /əv/, because both are the same word
Both are strong, /hæv/, because both follow “I”
The auxiliary keeps /hæv/ and the main verb is weak
quests.correctAnswer: The main verb “have” keeps /hæv/; the auxiliary “have” is weak, /əv/
quests.hint: Ask which “have” is the main verb and which one only helps another verb.
quests.explanation: A main verb carries meaning and keeps its strong form: “I have a car”, /hæv/. An auxiliary only helps another verb, so it is weak: “I have seen it”, /əv/. The sound difference signals the grammatical role. This is why “have” is not reduced everywhere.
quests.phoneticRule: Main-verb “have” is strong (/hæv/), whereas auxiliary “have” is weak (/əv/), so reduction depends on the word’s grammatical function.
quests.spokenForm: Jonas, I hæv a car and I əv seen it

quests.instruction: In “Selma, I do like it, I just can’t afford it”, why might “do” carry a strong form?
quests.word: Selma, I do like it, I just can’t afford it
quests.textToSpeak: Selma, I do like it, I just can’t afford it
options: The speaker stresses “do” to contradict an assumption that they do not like it
“do” is strong before any verb in English
“do” is a content word in this sentence
Strong forms are used only when a speaker is talking slowly or reading aloud to an audience
quests.correctAnswer: The speaker stresses “do” to contradict an assumption that they do not like it
quests.hint: Ask what the speaker wants the listener to understand from the extra weight on one small word.
quests.explanation: Auxiliary “do” is normally weak, but it can be stressed for emphasis or contrast. Here the speaker corrects a possible impression that they do not like it, so “do” takes the beat: /duː/. The rest of the sentence keeps its normal reductions. Emphasis, not speed, produces the strong form.
quests.phoneticRule: A normally weak auxiliary takes its strong form under contrastive or emphatic stress, which signals a correction.
quests.spokenForm: Selma, I DOO like it, I just can’t afford it

quests.instruction: In “Mind you, ten bags is plenty”, which change is coalescence and which is assimilation?
quests.word: Mind you, ten bags is plenty
quests.textToSpeak: Mind you, ten bags is plenty
options: “mind you” is assimilation (/d/ → [j]), and “ten bags” is coalescence (/n/ + /b/ → /m/)
Both are coalescence, because both create a new sound
Both are assimilation, because both change a final consonant
“mind you” is coalescence (/d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/); “ten bags” is assimilation (/n/ → [m])
quests.correctAnswer: “mind you” is coalescence (/d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/); “ten bags” is assimilation (/n/ → [m])
quests.hint: Ask whether two sounds fuse into one new sound, or one sound keeps its identity but changes its place.
quests.explanation: In “mind you”, /d/ and /j/ are both replaced by a single /dʒ/: coalescence. In “ten bags”, the /n/ is still a nasal, but its place changes from the tongue tip to the lips: assimilation. Both feel like “the sound changed”, but only one involves two sounds becoming one. That is the subtle point.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence replaces two segments with one new segment, whereas assimilation changes a feature of one segment while both segments remain.
quests.spokenForm: Min-joo, tem bags is plenty

quests.instruction: Why is “miss you” coalescence but “miss Sheila” assimilation in “Pia, I’ll miss you and miss Sheila too”?
quests.word: Pia, I’ll miss you and miss Sheila too
quests.textToSpeak: Pia, I’ll miss you and miss Sheila too
options: In “miss you” the /s/ is omitted, and in “miss Sheila” it is linked onto the /ʃ/ that follows
Both are coalescence, because both produce /ʃ/
“miss you” fuses /s/ + /j/ into one /ʃ/; in “miss Sheila” /s/ becomes /ʃ/ and both /ʃ/ remain
Both are assimilation, because both involve /s/
quests.correctAnswer: “miss you” fuses /s/ + /j/ into one /ʃ/; in “miss Sheila” /s/ becomes /ʃ/ and both /ʃ/ remain
quests.hint: Count how many original sounds survive in each result.
quests.explanation: In “miss you”, /s/ and /j/ disappear and one /ʃ/ takes their place. In “miss Sheila”, the final /s/ changes to /ʃ/ to match the /ʃ/ that begins “Sheila”, and both /ʃ/ sounds remain, so one long /ʃ/ is heard. The outputs sound similar, but one merges two inputs and the other adapts one to the other.
quests.phoneticRule: Both processes can produce /ʃ/; coalescence merges two inputs into one segment, whereas assimilation adapts one segment to a neighbour that stays.
quests.spokenForm: Pia, I’ll mi-shoo and mish Sheila too

quests.instruction: Which change in “Elio, would you mind moving that bag?” is coalescence?
quests.word: Elio, would you mind moving that bag
quests.textToSpeak: Elio, would you mind moving that bag
options: “mind moving” → [m], where the /d/ assimilates to the /m/
“that bag” → [p], where the /t/ assimilates to the /b/
“would you” → /dʒ/, where /d/ and /j/ fuse into one sound
None: all three changes are assimilation
quests.correctAnswer: “would you” → /dʒ/, where /d/ and /j/ fuse into one sound
quests.hint: Find the change in which two sounds become one new sound.
quests.explanation: “Would you” has /d/ + /j/, which fuse into /dʒ/: coalescence. “Mind moving” has a /d/ before /m/, and “that bag” has a /t/ before /b/; in both a final alveolar adapts toward the following sound, which is assimilation. So one question contains one coalescence and two assimilations.
quests.phoneticRule: A sentence may contain several changes, and only the one that fuses two sounds into a new one counts as coalescence.
quests.spokenForm: Elio, wou-ja mine moving thap bag

quests.instruction: In “Greta, that’s not much fun”, the /t/ in “not” is heard as a quick closure with no release. Which statement is right?
quests.word: Greta, that’s not much fun
quests.textToSpeak: Greta, that’s not much fun
options: It is reduced (unreleased), not elided, because a closure is still made
It is elided, because no puff of air is heard
It has become a /k/ because “much” follows
It is linked onto “much”, so the /t/ moves to the start of the next word entirely
quests.correctAnswer: It is reduced (unreleased), not elided, because a closure is still made
quests.hint: Ask whether any trace of a /t/ closure remains, even without a burst.
quests.explanation: An unreleased or glottalised /t/ still involves a closure: the vowel before it stops abruptly, even though no puff of air follows. Elision would leave no closure at all. So the /t/ in “not much” can be reduced without being removed. The distinction is subtle but audible.
quests.phoneticRule: An unreleased /t/ retains a closure and is a reduction, whereas an elided /t/ leaves no closure; the two should not be conflated.
quests.spokenForm: Greta, that’s noʔ much fun

quests.instruction: How do the /t/ sounds in “last night” and “hot night” differ in “Kiran, the last night was a hot night”?
quests.word: Kiran, the last night was a hot night
quests.textToSpeak: Kiran, the last night was a hot night
options: Both lose the /t/ entirely
Both keep a fully released /t/
“last night” often loses its /t/ (after /s/); “hot night” keeps a reduced closure (after a vowel)
“last night” keeps a reduced closure, while “hot night” loses the /t/ entirely, since vowels delete /t/
quests.correctAnswer: “last night” often loses its /t/ (after /s/); “hot night” keeps a reduced closure (after a vowel)
quests.hint: Look at what comes right before the /t/ in each phrase, and let that decide the outcome.
quests.explanation: After /s/ the /t/ is in a crowded cluster and is often omitted: “las’ night”. After a vowel there is no cluster, so the /t/ is more often reduced to a closure or a throat stop than deleted. The same /t/ and the same next sound lead to different outcomes because of the sound before the /t/.
quests.phoneticRule: The preceding sound determines the outcome: /t/ after /s/ is often omitted, whereas /t/ after a vowel is usually kept as a reduced closure.
quests.spokenForm: Kiran, the las’ night was a hoʔ night

quests.instruction: What is the best clue that a /t/ is unreleased rather than elided in “Willa, it was quite late”?
quests.word: Willa, it was quite late
quests.textToSpeak: Willa, it was quite late
options: The vowel before it is long and open
A strong burst of air follows the /t/
The next word begins with a vowel
The vowel before it stops abruptly, as if the mouth closes for a /t/
quests.correctAnswer: The vowel before it stops abruptly, as if the mouth closes for a /t/
quests.hint: Listen to how the vowel in “quite” ends.
quests.explanation: When a /t/ is unreleased, the vowel before it is cut off by a closure, which gives a clipped sound. When a /t/ is elided there is no such cutoff and the vowel runs straight on. A burst of air would mean a fully released /t/. So the end of the vowel is the best clue.
quests.phoneticRule: A clipped vowel ending signals an unreleased or glottal /t/, whereas an elided /t/ leaves the vowel to run on without a closure.
quests.spokenForm: Willa, it was quiʔ late

quests.instruction: What does “’s” stand for in both “it’s got” and “it’s gone” in “Dev, it’s got a crack and it’s gone dark”?
quests.word: Dev, it’s got a crack and it’s gone dark
quests.textToSpeak: Dev, it’s got a crack and it’s gone dark
options: “is” in both, because “it is” is the usual form
“is” in “it’s got” and “has” in “it’s gone”
“does” in both, because “it” takes “does” in questions and negatives
“has” in both, because “got” and “gone” are past participles
quests.correctAnswer: “has” in both, because “got” and “gone” are past participles
quests.hint: Check whether “got” and “gone” are past participles, then decide what the contraction hides.
quests.explanation: “Got” and “gone” are past participles, so the contraction stands for the auxiliary “has” in both: “it has got a crack”, “it has gone dark”. A learner who hears /ɪts/ might assume “it is”, but “it is got” and “it is gone” would need a different structure. The sound is the same; the grammar decides.
quests.phoneticRule: Contracted ’s is “has” when followed by a past participle, and the participle form is the cue to its meaning.
quests.spokenForm: Dev, itsgot a crack and itsgone dark

quests.instruction: What do the three “’d” forms stand for in “Pia, I’d forgotten that you’d said you’d call”?
quests.word: Pia, I’d forgotten that you’d said you’d call
quests.textToSpeak: Pia, I’d forgotten that you’d said you’d call
options: “had”, “had” and “would”
“would”, “had” and “would”
“had”, “would” and “would”
“would”, “would” and “had”
quests.correctAnswer: “had”, “had” and “would”
quests.hint: Sort the verbs “forgotten”, “said” and “call” by form, and match each ’d to its partner.
quests.explanation: “Forgotten” and “said” are past participles, so the first two “’d” forms are “had”. “Call” is a base form, so the last “’d” is “would”. The three contractions sound identical, /d/, so grammar is the only guide. Advanced listening depends on tracking the verb that follows.
quests.phoneticRule: A past participle after contracted /d/ signals “had”, and a base verb signals “would”, even within a single sentence.
quests.spokenForm: Pia, I’d forgotten that yood said yood call

quests.instruction: What do the two “’s” forms stand for in “Yusuf, Dana’s coming and Dana’s car is outside”?
quests.word: Yusuf, Dana’s coming and Dana’s car is outside
quests.textToSpeak: Yusuf, Dana’s coming and Dana’s car is outside
options: The first is “is” (a contraction), and the second marks possession
Both are “is”
Both mark possession
The first marks possession, and the second is “is”
quests.correctAnswer: The first is “is” (a contraction), and the second marks possession
quests.hint: Look at what follows each “’s”: a verb ending in “-ing”, or a noun.
quests.explanation: “Dana’s coming” needs the verb “is” before “coming”, so the first “’s” is a contraction. “Dana’s car” has a noun after the “’s”, so it marks possession. The two sound identical, /z/. The only difference is the word that follows. That is why context rather than sound resolves the meaning.
quests.phoneticRule: Identical /z/ sounds can be a contracted verb (“is”) or a possessive marker; the following word class decides which.
quests.spokenForm: Yusuf, Danaz coming and Danaz car is outside

quests.instruction: Which of these is not a normal pronunciation of “because” in “Mara, I stayed because it was raining”?
quests.word: Mara, I stayed because it was raining
quests.textToSpeak: Mara, I stayed because it was raining
options: “bi-kŏz”, with a short first vowel
“bə-kəz”, with both vowels weak
“kəz”, with the first syllable dropped
“bee-cause-uh”, with an extra final vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “bee-cause-uh”, with an extra final vowel
quests.hint: Three of these are everyday variants; one adds a sound that does not belong.
quests.explanation: “Because” can be said with a short /ɪ/, with a schwa, or reduced to “’cos”, depending on speed and style. All of these are normal. Adding a final vowel, as in “bee-cause-uh”, is not a pattern of native speech and would sound unusual. Normal variation is wide, but it is not unlimited.
quests.phoneticRule: Normal variation in function words includes vowel reduction and syllable loss, but not the addition of extra segments.
quests.spokenForm: Mara, I stayed bee-cause-uh it was raining

quests.instruction: Which statement about “and” in “Noor, salt and pepper are on the table” is accurate?
quests.word: Noor, salt and pepper are on the table
quests.textToSpeak: Noor, salt and pepper are on the table
options: Only /ænd/ is correct, and the others are mistakes
All of /ænd/, /ənd/, /ən/ and /n/ occur by speed and style; none is an error
Only /n/ is correct in fast speech, and the full form is a mistake in any style
/ænd/ is incorrect after a noun, but correct after a verb
quests.correctAnswer: All of /ænd/, /ənd/, /ən/ and /n/ occur by speed and style; none is an error
quests.hint: Think about how many forms an unstressed word can have in everyday speech.
quests.explanation: “And” is one of the most reduced words in English. Careful speech may keep /ænd/, normal speech uses /ənd/ or /ən/, and fast speech reduces it to /n/. None of these is an error. They are variants along a scale of speed and formality. Recognising the whole range is part of advanced listening.
quests.phoneticRule: A frequent function word has a range of acceptable forms, from the full /ænd/ to the reduced /n/, selected by speed and style.
quests.spokenForm: Noor, salt n pepper are on the table

quests.instruction: A learner says “Umar, ask him about it” as “ask… HIM… about it”, with a strong /h/ and pauses. Is this wrong?
quests.word: Umar, ask him about it
quests.textToSpeak: Umar, ask him about it
options: Wrong, because the /h/ must be dropped in every case
Not wrong, but it sounds careful or emphatic; the usual fast form is “as-kim”
Wrong, because pronouns cannot be stressed
Right in every situation, so the fast form is incorrect
quests.correctAnswer: Not wrong, but it sounds careful or emphatic; the usual fast form is “as-kim”
quests.hint: Think about how a careful, emphatic style differs from an ordinary fast one.
quests.explanation: A clear /h/ and a pause give “him” prominence, as if the speaker were contrasting him with someone else. It is not incorrect, but it is marked, and it can sound stiff or insistent. The unmarked form in fast speech has a dropped /h/ and a link: “as-kim”. Variation of this kind should be judged by context, not by correctness.
quests.phoneticRule: Careful or emphatic pronunciation is a marked variant, not an error; the unmarked fast form shows /h/ dropping and linking.
quests.spokenForm: Umar, as-kim about it

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Morning, did you eat? Not yet, I’m going to grab a bite”?
quests.word: Morning, did you eat? Not yet, I’m going to grab a bite
quests.textToSpeak: Morning, did you eat? Not yet, I’m going to grab a bite
options: A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), a /tʃ/ blend (“not yet”), and “gonna” (“going to”)
A /tʃ/ blend (“did you”), a /dʒ/ blend (“not yet”), and “gonna”
Two /dʒ/ blends and a dropped /h/
A /tʃ/ blend (“did you”), elision in “not yet”, and “wanna”
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), a /tʃ/ blend (“not yet”), and “gonna” (“going to”)
quests.hint: Scan each boundary for a /d/ or /t/ meeting a “y” sound, and spot the shortened verb phrase.
quests.explanation: “Did you” has /d/ + /j/, so it blends into /dʒ/. “Not yet” has /t/ + /j/, so it blends into /tʃ/: “no-chet”. “Going to” is reduced to “gonna”, and “grab a” links. A short exchange can therefore contain two different blends and an informal reduction. Naming each one correctly is the skill.
quests.phoneticRule: A two-line exchange can include blends with different results and informal reductions, each determined by its own neighbouring sounds.
quests.spokenForm: Morning, di-ja eat? No-chet, I’m gonna gra-ba bite

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Of course, let me move it so you can sit down”?
quests.word: Of course, let me move it so you can sit down
quests.textToSpeak: Of course, let me move it so you can sit down
options: A /dʒ/ blend in “let me”, “gonna” in “move it”, and a strong “can”
“lemme” (informal “let me”), a link in “move it”, and a weak “can”
A link in “let me”, a dropped /h/ in “move it”, and a strong “can” in “you can sit”
“lemme”, gemination in “move it”, and a /tʃ/ blend in “so you”
quests.correctAnswer: “lemme” (informal “let me”), a link in “move it”, and a weak “can”
quests.hint: Check the three stretches: “let me”, “move it” and “you can”.
quests.explanation: “Let me” is often said as “lemme”, with the /t/ lost. “Move it” joins a final /v/ onto a vowel: “moo-vit”. “Can” is weak, /kən/. So one polite offer shows an informal fused form, a consonant-to-vowel link and a weak auxiliary together.
quests.phoneticRule: A short offer may combine an informal fused form, a consonant-to-vowel link and a weak auxiliary.
quests.spokenForm: Of course, lemme moo-vit so you kən sit down

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Tara, did he say he’d call? He should’ve, but he didn’t”?
quests.word: Tara, did he say he’d call? He should’ve, but he didn’t
quests.textToSpeak: Tara, did he say he’d call? He should’ve, but he didn’t
options: A dropped /h/ with a link (“did he”), a contraction (“he’d”), and a weak “’ve” (“should’ve”)
A /dʒ/ blend (“did he”), a contraction (“he’d”), and a strong “have”, with all words separated
A dropped /h/ (“did he”), a /j/ glide (“he’d call”), and “should of”
Gemination (“did he”), a contraction, and an omitted /t/ in “didn’t”
quests.correctAnswer: A dropped /h/ with a link (“did he”), a contraction (“he’d”), and a weak “’ve” (“should’ve”)
quests.hint: Go through the dialogue boundary by boundary and ask what each one triggers.
quests.explanation: In “did he”, the /h/ is dropped and the /d/ links: “di-dee”. “He’d” is a contraction (here “he would”), and “should’ve” is /ˈʃʊdəv/ with a weak “’ve”. So a short dialogue combines /h/ dropping with linking, contraction and weak-form reduction. Each is independent of the others.
quests.phoneticRule: A dialogue turn can combine dropped /h/ with linking, a contraction and a weak “’ve”, without any interaction among them.
quests.spokenForm: Tara, di-dee say heed call? He shou-dəv, but he di-dnt

quests.instruction: Which delivery has natural rhythm for “Noor, I think we should get the earlier train”?
quests.word: Noor, I think we should get the earlier train
quests.textToSpeak: Noor, I think we should get the earlier train
options: Equal beats on every word, with a clear pause after each
Beats on I, we, the and train, with the content words squeezed
Beats only on the first and last words, with everything else flat and spoken at the same speed
Beats on think, get, earlier and train, with the small words squeezed between them
quests.correctAnswer: Beats on think, get, earlier and train, with the small words squeezed between them
quests.hint: Find the words that carry the plan and the words that only connect them.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “think”, “get”, “earlier” and “train”. The small words “I”, “we”, “should” and “the” are compressed between the beats, and “the” is /ði/ before the vowel of “earlier”. This produces a natural rhythm. Equal beats would slow the sentence and hide the plan.
quests.phoneticRule: Natural rhythm places beats on the content words and compresses the pronouns, modals and articles between them.
quests.spokenForm: NOor, I THINK wi shəd GET thee EARlier TRAIN

quests.instruction: In “Jonas, I’m going to see her tomorrow at ten”, which part is compressed most?
quests.word: Jonas, I’m going to see her tomorrow at ten
quests.textToSpeak: Jonas, I’m going to see her tomorrow at ten
options: “see” and “ten”, which carry beats
“tomorrow”, which is the longest word
“I’m going to” and “her”, which are unstressed and short
“at”, because prepositions are never stressed
quests.correctAnswer: “I’m going to” and “her”, which are unstressed and short
quests.hint: Look for the words that could be squeezed without losing the message.
quests.explanation: “I’m going to” is reduced to “I’m gonna”, and “her” is weak and loses its /h/. Neither carries the information. “See”, “tomorrow” and “ten” carry the beats. Length is not the same as stress, and a preposition can be stressed in some contexts. So compression follows function, not word length.
quests.phoneticRule: Compression follows grammatical function and information value, so auxiliary strings and unstressed pronouns are squeezed, whatever their length.
quests.spokenForm: JOnas, I’m gonna SEE er toMORrow at TEN

quests.instruction: Which delivery of “Luca, could you pass me the salt and pepper?” sounds most natural?
quests.word: Luca, could you pass me the salt and pepper
quests.textToSpeak: Luca, could you pass me the salt and pepper
options: “COULD YOU PASS ME THE SALT AND PEPPER”: every word strong
“could you pass me the SALT and PEPPER”: strong only at the end
“cou-ja PASS me thuh SALT n PEPper”: a blend, with beats on pass, salt and pepper
“cou-ja pass me the salt-n-pepper”: all words flat and equal, with no beats and no pauses
quests.correctAnswer: “cou-ja PASS me thuh SALT n PEPper”: a blend, with beats on pass, salt and pepper
quests.hint: Pick the version with a blend in the first words and clear beats on the key nouns.
quests.explanation: “Could you” blends into /dʒə/, the key words “pass”, “salt” and “pepper” carry beats, and “me”, “the” and “and” are squeezed. An all-strong delivery sounds slow, and a flat delivery has no rhythm. The natural form has both a blend and a beat pattern. That is what integrated rhythm sounds like.
quests.phoneticRule: A natural request combines a blend with a rhythmic pattern in which only the content words carry beats.
quests.spokenForm: LUca, cou-ja PASS me thuh SALT n PEPper

quests.instruction: Which statement about the /t/ in “get up” in “Nell, get up and put the water on” is accurate?
quests.word: Nell, get up and put the water on
quests.textToSpeak: Nell, get up and put the water on
options: It is a clear released /t/ in every accent, as in careful speech, in dictionaries and in everyday talk
In General American it is often a flap [ɾ]; in many British accents, a /t/ or glottal stop
It becomes /d/ in British English only
It is omitted in every accent
quests.correctAnswer: In General American it is often a flap [ɾ]; in many British accents, a /t/ or glottal stop
quests.hint: Think about how different accents treat /t/ between vowels.
quests.explanation: In General American a /t/ between vowels, as in “get up” or “water”, is often a quick flap [ɾ], sounding like a /d/. In many British accents the same /t/ may be a clear /t/ or a glottal stop. Both are normal. The variation is accent-dependent, so a learner should recognise both and not treat one as an error.
quests.phoneticRule: Intervocalic /t/ varies by accent: flapped [ɾ] in General American, and [t] or glottal [ʔ] in many British accents.
quests.spokenForm: Nell, ge-ɾup and put the waɾer on

quests.instruction: Which statement is accurate for “saw a” and “drama about” in “Fiona, I saw a drama about the law”?
quests.word: Fiona, I saw a drama about the law
quests.textToSpeak: Fiona, I saw a drama about the law
options: An /r/ appears in all accents because both words end in vowels and the next word begins with one
An /r/ appears only in rhotic accents
In non-rhotic accents an intrusive /r/ may appear at both; rhotic accents do not use it
An intrusive /r/ is required by grammar
quests.correctAnswer: In non-rhotic accents an intrusive /r/ may appear at both; rhotic accents do not use it
quests.hint: Check whether the accent drops final “r” before consonants, and whether it adds /r/ before vowels.
quests.explanation: In non-rhotic accents, speakers who use intrusive /r/ may insert it after /ɔː/ and /ə/ before a vowel: “saw-ra”, “drama-rabout”. Rhotic accents such as most American English do not use it. It is optional and accent-dependent, not a grammatical rule. Recognition is the goal.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ is optional and confined to non-rhotic accents; rhotic accents do not insert it.
quests.spokenForm: Fiona, I saw-ra drama-rabout the law

quests.instruction: A British speaker says “water” with a glottal stop, and an American speaker says it with a flap. Which statement is fair?
quests.word: Hamza, fill the water bottle before we leave
quests.textToSpeak: Hamza, fill the water bottle before we leave
options: The glottal stop is an error in all accents
The flap is an error in all accents
Both are normal variants of /t/ in their accents; neither is an error
Only a fully released /t/ is correct in careful speech anywhere in the world
quests.correctAnswer: Both are normal variants of /t/ in their accents; neither is an error
quests.hint: Think about whether pronunciation variation is the same as pronunciation error.
quests.explanation: Glottalisation is a normal realisation of /t/ in many British accents, and flapping is a normal realisation in General American. Neither is an error. A fully released /t/ is also normal but is more careful or marked in these positions. Variation across accents is part of connected speech, and a good listener accepts it.
quests.phoneticRule: Accent variants of /t/ (flap, glottal stop, released stop) are all acceptable realisations in their own varieties.
quests.spokenForm: Hamza, fill the waʔer bottle before we leave

quests.instruction: A friend invites you to the cinema and you decline politely and quickly. Which spoken form of “I’d love to, but I’ve got to work tomorrow” is the most natural?
quests.word: I’d love to, but I’ve got to work tomorrow
quests.textToSpeak: I’d love to, but I’ve got to work tomorrow
options: “I would love to, but I have got to work tomorrow”, all words strong
“I’d love too, but I’ve gonna work tomorrow”: “gonna” in place of “gotta”
“I’d love to, but I’ve got-too work tomorrow”: a strong “to”
“I’d love tuh, but I’ve gotta work tomorrow”, with a weak “to” and “gotta”
quests.correctAnswer: “I’d love tuh, but I’ve gotta work tomorrow”, with a weak “to” and “gotta”
quests.hint: Choose the form that keeps the contractions and the informal reduction in the right place.
quests.explanation: “I’d” is a contraction of “I would”, “to” at the end of “love to” is weak, and “got to” is reduced to “gotta”. Using “gonna” would change the meaning. A natural, quick decline therefore combines two contractions and one informal reduction, all in the right places.
quests.phoneticRule: A polite spoken refusal uses contractions and the informal “gotta”, and the reductions must match their source phrases.
quests.spokenForm: I’d love tuh, but I’ve gotta work tomorrow

quests.instruction: In a stuffy room you ask, “Alright if I open the window, it’s warm in here?” Which delivery is the most natural?
quests.word: Alright if I open the window, it’s warm in here
quests.textToSpeak: Alright if I open the window, it’s warm in here
options: Slow and separated: every word strong, with a pause after each
Linked and light: “alrigh-ti-fai ope-nthe window, it’s warm in here”
Reduced but flat: no beats, so the request sounds like a murmur
Fast but unlinked: weak vowels, with clear breaks between all words
quests.correctAnswer: Linked and light: “alrigh-ti-fai ope-nthe window, it’s warm in here”
quests.hint: Think about which version links consonants to vowels and still keeps clear beats.
quests.explanation: A natural request is linked (“alrigh-ti-fai”, “ope-nthe”), light on the function words, and clear on the content words “open”, “window” and “warm”. A slow delivery sounds formal, a flat one is hard to hear, and an unlinked one sounds jerky. The best version sounds relaxed but still audible.
quests.phoneticRule: A natural informal request is linked and reduced, but it keeps clear beats on the content words so it remains audible.
quests.spokenForm: Alrigh-ti-fai ope-nthe window, it’s warm in here

quests.instruction: You are leaving a quick voicemail for a friend. Which line is the most natural?
quests.word: Evening, it’s me, call me back when you get a chance
quests.textToSpeak: Evening, it’s me, call me back when you get a chance
options: “Evening, it is me, call me back when you get a chance”, all words strong and separate
“Evening, it’s me, call me back when you ge-ta chance”: linked “get a”, with weak “you” and “when”
“Evening, it’s me, call me back when you get-chance”: “a” is dropped
“Evening, it’s me, call me back wen yoo get uh chance”: every word with a full vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “Evening, it’s me, call me back when you ge-ta chance”: linked “get a”, with weak “you” and “when”
quests.hint: Choose the version that links “get a” and weakens the small words without dropping any.
quests.explanation: “Get a” links its /t/ onto the weak “a”: “ge-ta”. “When” and “you” are weak: /wən/, /jə/. The key words “call”, “back” and “chance” carry the beats. A voicemail is spoken quickly and informally, so this form is the natural one. Dropping “a” would change the grammar.
quests.phoneticRule: A casual voicemail keeps linking and weak forms while preserving all of its words and the beats on the content words.
quests.spokenForm: Evening, it’s me, call me back when you ge-ta chance

quests.instruction: In a fast “Zeke, I kept my ticket”, you hear “kep’ my”. Which label is best for the /t/?
quests.word: Zeke, I kept my ticket
quests.textToSpeak: Zeke, I kept my ticket
options: Assimilation: the /t/ has become /p/
Coalescence: the /t/ and the /m/ have fused into a single new sound
Linking: the /t/ has moved onto “my”
Elision: the /t/ is absent and no substitute sound appears
quests.correctAnswer: Elision: the /t/ is absent and no substitute sound appears
quests.hint: Ask whether the /t/ has been replaced by another sound or has simply gone.
quests.explanation: “Kept” ends in /pt/ before /m/, so the /t/ is often omitted: “kep’ my”. The /p/ was already there; no new sound appears in the /t/’s place. That makes it elision, not assimilation (a changed sound), coalescence (a fused sound) or linking (a moved sound). Naming the process correctly is the final skill of this level.
quests.phoneticRule: To distinguish processes, check whether the segment is absent (elision), changed (assimilation), fused (coalescence) or moved (linking).
quests.spokenForm: Zeke, I kep’ my ticket

quests.instruction: In “Mara, the black cat is on the mat”, one long /k/ is heard in “black cat”. Which label is best?
quests.word: Mara, the black cat is on the mat
quests.textToSpeak: Mara, the black cat is on the mat
options: Elision: one /k/ is omitted
Assimilation: the /k/ moves to the lips
Gemination: two identical /k/ sounds are held as one
Coalescence: the two /k/ sounds fuse into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: Gemination: two identical /k/ sounds are held as one
quests.hint: Check whether the two sounds are identical and whether the result is longer than a single /k/.
quests.explanation: “Black” ends in /k/ and “cat” begins with /k/. The closure is held and released once, giving a longer /k/: gemination. Elision would leave a single normal /k/, assimilation needs different sounds, and coalescence requires a /j/ trigger. So the length of the held consonant identifies the process.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination is identified by two identical consonants realised as one longer consonant, unlike elision, assimilation or coalescence.
quests.spokenForm: Mara, the blak-kat is on the mat

quests.instruction: Which labels fit the two /r/ sounds in “Ines, the idea of it is far away”?
quests.word: Ines, the idea of it is far away
quests.textToSpeak: Ines, the idea of it is far away
options: An intrusive /r/ in “idea of”, and a linking /r/ in “far away”
Linking in both, because the /r/ is heard before a vowel each time
Intrusive in both, because both are before vowels
Intrusive in “far away”, and linking in “idea of”
quests.correctAnswer: An intrusive /r/ in “idea of”, and a linking /r/ in “far away”
quests.hint: Use the spelling of “idea” and “far” to tell which /r/ is written and which is added.
quests.explanation: “Idea” has no “r” in the spelling, so the /r/ before “of” is intrusive, and it is accent-dependent. “Far” is spelled with “r”, so the /r/ before “away” is linking. The two sound the same in a non-rhotic accent, but they have different sources. Naming them separately completes the picture.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive and linking /r/ sound the same, but the first has no spelled “r” and the second does.
quests.spokenForm: Ines, the idea-rof it is far-raway
